claim: In eval-driven development, evals are the working spec: developers maintain golden-set datasets as the regression baseline, change a prompt/model and rerun the eval suite (catching e.g. a tone score dropping 0.85 to 0.72), and CI blocks the change automatically if any metric falls below its gate threshold.
quote: If any metric falls below its threshold at any gate, the CI pipeline blocks the change automatically ... tone score dropped from 0.85 to 0.72 ... production traces that reveal new edge cases get added to golden sets

claim: A practitioner eval pipeline separates offline CI evals (LLM judge plus human review) from online production evals running lightweight deterministic checks under 50ms with 5% async sampling for deeper judging, handles judge flakiness by running twice with swapped positions to detect bias, and gates CI on minPassRate 0.95 / maxRegressions 0.
quote: Run lightweight evals on every response (< 50ms overhead) ... Async: sample 5% for deeper LLM-as-Judge evaluation ... Run twice with swapped positions to eliminate position bias ... minPassRate: 0.95 / maxRegressions: 0

claim: To tame flaky judges, teams define pass bands rather than single thresholds, avoid gating when the judge confidence is below the 0.41-0.60 moderate band, recalibrate the judge monthly or when divergence climbs past ~20-25%, and report pass@k since a 70%-per-trial agent reads ~97% on pass@3 but ~34% on pass^3.
quote: Below the 0.41-0.60 'moderate' band, do not gate on the judge ... a 70%-per-trial agent reads as ~97% on pass@3 but ~34% on pass^3 ... trigger out-of-cycle when you ... see divergence climb past ~20-25%

claim: When LLM-as-judge scorers are flaky or nondeterministic, the guidance is to design for variance rather than pretend determinism: control judge temperature, rerun borderline cases, and reserve repeated judging or ensembles for high-impact decisions.
quote: When judges are flaky or nondeterministic, the goal is not to pretend they are deterministic, but to design for variance: keep the judge temperature controlled when possible, rerun borderline cases, and reserve repeated judging or ensembles for high-impact decisions

claim: Manual vibe-checking fails at scale: informal evaluation plateaus into a whack-a-mole loop, and Hamel's framework prescribes three levels (programmatic unit-test asserts, human+model eval, A/B testing) with model-based judges validated against human labels.
quote: limited visibility into the AI system's effectiveness across tasks beyond vibe checks ... You must continue doing periodic exercises to monitor the model and human agreement

claim: G-Eval uses chain-of-thought-generated evaluation steps plus a form-filling, log-probability-weighted scoring paradigm and achieved the highest Spearman correlation with human judgments (0.514) on SummEval, but does not directly eliminate verbosity or self-preference bias.
quote: G-Eval achieved the highest Spearman correlation with human judgments (0.514), outperforming all baselines ... G-Eval doesn't directly eliminate narcissistic bias

claim: Self-preference bias is formally measurable as the gap in an evaluator favoring itself; on Chatbot Arena (33k dialogues, 8 LLM judges) GPT-4 showed the highest self-preference bias score of ~0.520 (favorable recall 0.945 vs unfavorable 0.425).
quote: GPT-4 exhibits the highest bias ... a self-preference bias score of approximately 0.520 ... recall rates of 0.945 (favorable cases) and 0.425 (unfavorable cases)

claim: No judge is uniformly reliable: a RAND study found consistency broke down on formatting changes and paraphrasing, JudgeBiasBench found frontier models exceeding 50% error on advanced bias tests, and 80% human-agreement and 50% bias-error findings coexist rather than conflict.
quote: No judge evaluated by the RAND Corporation's research team was uniformly reliable across benchmarks ... Frontier models exceeded 50% error rates on advanced bias tests ... The 80% agreement finding and the 50% error rate on bias benchmarks are not in conflict

claim: LLM-evaluators carry documented position bias (claude-v1 biased toward first position 70% of the time), verbosity bias (claude-v1 and gpt-3.5 preferred the longer response >90% of the time), and self-enhancement (gpt-4 +10%, claude-v1 +25% self win-rate), with poor sensitivity on factual-consistency tasks, so they are not reliable enough to systematically replace human judgment.
quote: Both claude-v1 and gpt-3.5 preferred the longer response more than 90% of the time ... Gpt-4 favored itself with a 10% higher win rate while claude-v1 favored itself with a 25% higher win rate ... they're not reliable enough to systematically replace human judgments

claim: Direct scoring by LLMs is misaligned with humans in a way calibration cannot fix; reframing evaluation as pairwise preference ranking (PAIRS) produces rankings inherently more aligned with human judgment, which is why pairwise comparison is favored for subjective evals.
quote: A systematic analysis of LLMs used as direct scorers revealed a misalignment between LLM and human evaluators, which cannot be effectively mitigated by applying calibration techniques

claim: 2026 practitioner guidance enumerates five named LLM-judge biases (position, verbosity, self-preference, format, calibration drift) and treats 'never use the same model as judge and candidate' as a cardinal rule since self-preference adds 10-25% uniform bias.
quote: position, verbosity, self-preference, format, and calibration drift ... never use the same model as judge and candidate, as self-preference adds 10 to 25 percent uniform bias

claim: Ragas defines four core RAG metrics: faithfulness, answer relevancy, context precision, and context recall, splitting evaluation across retriever and generator.
quote: Faithfulness measures factual consistency of the answer with the retrieved context; answer relevancy measures alignment between answer and question; context precision measures whether relevant chunks are ranked highly; context recall measures how much of the ground truth is captured.

claim: Ragas metrics carry diagnostic benchmark targets: faithfulness ~0.75, answer relevancy ~0.8, context precision ~0.7, context recall ~0.8, with the overall Ragas score being their mean.
quote: faithfulness (0.75 benchmark), answer relevancy (0.8), context precision (0.7), and context recall (0.8)... the ragas score is the mean of Faithfulness, Answer relevancy, Context recall, and Context precision.

claim: Agent evaluation in 2026 splits into three levels (end-to-end task success, trajectory-level path analysis, component-level tests) with core metrics tool correctness, task completion, step efficiency, and argument correctness.
quote: Tool Correctness... evaluates whether the agent called the right tool. Task Completion... uses an LLM to infer the user's goal... Step Efficiency measures whether agents avoid unnecessary tool invocations... Argument Correctness evaluates whether agents pass correct input parameters.

claim: DeepEval's G-Eval is a criteria-based LLM-as-judge metric using chain-of-thought to score outputs against any custom criteria like correctness, coherence or tone.
quote: G-Eval is a criteria-based metric using LLM-as-a-judge with chain-of-thought to evaluate LLM outputs based on any custom criteria, making it the most versatile metric type in DeepEval.

claim: LangSmith's agentevals package evaluates agent trajectories via four trajectory-match modes (strict, unordered, superset, subset) plus an LLM-as-judge trajectory evaluator.
quote: Strict Mode: exact match of messages and tool calls in the same order... Unordered Mode: identical tool calls in any order... Superset Mode: at least the reference tools (extras allowed)... Subset Mode: only tool calls that appear in the reference trajectory.

claim: LangChain's open-source agentevals package provides readymade evaluators for agent trajectories (the exact sequence of messages including tool calls) and integrates with LangSmith.
quote: Readymade evaluators for agent trajectories... evaluate the trajectory of your agent (the exact sequence of messages, including tool calls) by performing a trajectory match or by using an LLM judge.

claim: UK AISI's Inspect AI is built on Tasks/Datasets/Solvers/Scorers with first-class tool use, supporting ReAct, Deep Agent, and custom multi-agent architectures for agentic evals.

claim: Galileo offers named agentic metrics including Tool Selection Quality, Action Completion, Reasoning Coherence and Agent Efficiency, powered by Luna-2 small models running 10-20 metrics at sub-200ms latency.

claim: The three structural failure modes of static benchmarks are saturation (top models cluster near ceiling), contamination (test data leaks into training), and gameability (optimizing to the benchmark without real-world gains).
